old: The Buddha splits the accounting cleanly in SN 22.22: the five aggregates are the burden; craving is picking it up. The tangle is heavy by nature – even an arahant feels the first dart – and craving keeps us carrying it. Physics agrees that binding is literally heavy: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass; roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy. Matter weighs what its binding weighs. Light weighs nothing.
new: In SN 22.22 the five aggregates that make up the unified body-mind are the burden (even an arahant feels the first dart) of suffering, and craving is the process that keeps picking that burden up, so that you walk around unaware of the boulder on your back even as you keep making the payments to the Boulder Bank to keep it there (and thank God you can afford to!?). The tangle of the aggregates is what makes them heavy, which sounds counterintuitive since we don't imagine the whole can be more than the sum of its parts in that way. But "binding" is literally heavy in physics too: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy. Matter weighs what its binding weighs. Light weighs nothing.

old: I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha. The famous stanza I loved actually comes from the later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth, although the early Pāli texts offer closely related images. SN 22.95 compares form to foam, feeling to a bubble, perception to a mirage, and consciousness to a magic trick. Dhammapada 170 asks us to see the world as a bubble and mirage.
new: I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha, until I found out the famous stanza I loved comes from the much later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth. The early Pāli texts do give us some very similar kind of symbolism, though. SN 22.95 shows us how form is empty and always transforming, like foam, fleeting feeling is compared to a bubble, perception is only a mirage, and consciousness is basically the best magic trick. And Dhammapada 170 asks us to see the world as a bubble and mirage, so if you put it all together, you can certainly imagine that the basic idea of life being like a dream was originally intended.
